answer.bounds_note: TAM and SAM low and high move every input to its low or high at once, so they are outer bounds, not likely outcomes. SOM cases change only the share-of-search path.
answer.summary: SAM is about $176.7m a year at today's prices ($114.9m to $250.4m), and the business holds 0.74% of it. On its own retention, conversion and share of search it reaches $2.1m by year 3 in the base case ($2.0m to $2.2m), 0.92% of a SAM that grows 9.5% a year.

findings: Bottom-up SAM ($176.7m) and top-down ($158.5m) agree at a ratio of 1.11.
Search demand supports the buyer count in total (ratio 1.01), but Canada is flagged at 2.25: the English-only term set misses Quebec, and the gap narrows to 1.75 without it.
The UK has the lowest share of search (2.92% against 7.67% in the US) and it is falling (-0.49 points a year), with 33% of paid impression share lost to rank.
The US category campaign loses 38% of impression share to budget; winning back half of it is the high case.

US business counts move SAM the most ($37.8m swing). For year-3 SOM, annual spend per buyer, new customers from other channels, monthly churn and paying customers at window end each move it more than share of search today ($0.06m), because search brings about 20% of new customers.

unknowns: Canadian French-language search demand: not pulled (one paid call, offered).

Search Console clicks on non-brand variants of the category terms (best appointment booking software, best salon booking software: 701 clicks in the window) are left out of share of search, because the search volume pull did not include those phrases. Add them to the term list and the DataForSEO call to count them.
GA4 counts brand and category search sessions together, so the product-page sign-up rate may run a little high for category clicks.
Shopify and WooCommerce: not used; this is a subscription business, so customers and churn came from billing.
